keyVerseText: And he went a little further, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.
rootMeaning: The Greek verb προέρχομαι (proérchomai) is formed from the preposition πρό (pró), meaning 'before' or 'in front of,' combined with ἔρχομαι (érchomai), meaning 'to come' or 'to go.' This etymology highlights a fundamental sense of moving forward or going ahead, either spatially or temporally. Unlike the simple English glosses like 'go before' or 'advance,' the root sense conveys both precedence and progression, implying not only physical movement but also priority in time or rank.
usageInScripture: Across its nine occurrences, προέρχομαι consistently conveys the idea of going forward or preceding in place or time. It is translated variously as 'went before,' 'further,' 'outwent,' and 'he went forward,' reflecting a flexible but coherent semantic field centered on movement ahead or going on. This range shows the word's use in describing physical advancement, temporal precedence, or metaphorical progress, revealing its rich nuance beyond simple motion.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding προέρχομαι enriches our grasp of biblical narratives where movement and timing carry deep spiritual meaning. Its sense of going before or advancing can symbolize Christ's pioneering role in salvation history, as He moves ahead to fulfill the Father's will. This verb also reflects the believer's call to follow Christ's example of obedient progression, even in trials. Recognizing this word's original meaning helps believers appreciate the dynamic, forward-moving nature of God's redemptive plan and the faithful response it requires.
keyVerseReflection: In Matthew 26:39, 'And he went a little further, and fell on his face, and prayed,' the use of προέρχομαι emphasizes Jesus' deliberate movement forward into the will of the Father. This 'going a little further' is not just physical but signifies advancing toward the impending suffering and submission to God's plan. The word enriches the scene by portraying Jesus as actively progressing into the cup He asks to be removed, yet ultimately yielding to divine sovereignty.
